response.likely_cause: A shift in the screened patient population towards lower-risk individuals is the most probable cause, though evidence is weak due to the limited sample size of 50 scans. Referral rate dropped sharply while image quality metrics remained largely stable.
evidence: Referral rate decreased by -61.4% from 0.414 in training to 0.16 at the clinic.
Image quality remained nearly unchanged, with mean quality at 0.871 compared to 0.875 in training (-0.5% relative change).
Mean contrast showed minimal change from 0.0893 to 0.0891 (-0.2% relative change), and mean brightness shifted slightly from 0.402 to 0.382 (-4.8% relative change).
Mean resolution remained identical at 1020.0 px (0.0% relative change), while mean sharpness dropped slightly from 31.8 to 28.5 (-10.2% relative change).
Classifier referral score mean fell from 0.22 to 0.207 (-6.2% relative change).
Weekly sample size is low at 50 scans, resulting in an estimated catch rate of 67% with a wide uncertainty band of 48%-85% against the 90% baseline, rendering the evidence weak.
recommended_checks: Verify patient demographics and intake criteria at clinic US-UPD-01 during week 12 to identify any shift towards lower-risk or healthier cohorts.
Audit clinical triage and appointment scheduling logs for any recent modifications in screening indications.
Monitor scan volume and referral statistics over subsequent weeks to assess whether this pattern persists over a larger sample size.
